segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: When we got to this hill I saw a lot of dust, and I let the speeder go and I turned to investigate. I could see a white object sitting between those two bushes over there, and I had to come real slow because this was a messed-up road, had big rocks on and everything. I thought it was the kids from high school there, they were racing up here, and then maybe one of the teenagers had turned over.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the speeding object came to a stop, Zamora claims that he saw two figures in white coveralls emerge from a strange white UFO. He moved in slowly.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: I came up here on this road till I could find a flat spot where I could park my car. I got out the car and glanced down to the [arroyo] there, and I saw this white-looking object. It was sort of a big egg shape, bigger than a car. Those are the exact bushes that were there, and the craft was sitting right in between them too. So I started down to see what it was, and then I heard this big boom in the bottom, and the fire came off the bottom. So I started running behind my police car to take cover. I could feel the heat off of it, because it was windy like now. And then it gradually pulled up, up about 20, 30 feet, and stayed there for a while, and just took off.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His radio was dead. Zamora could only watch in awe as the object disappeared over the horizon. As soon as it was gone, the police radio crackled to life and Zamora called for backup. A New Mexico State Police unit quickly arrived.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: We came down here and we saw this big rock right down here, it was still on fire. And then we saw the imprints of the legs of the craft, and there was four of them. And then we saw these footprints on here.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By nightfall the FBI had arrived on scene and began gathering evidence.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: They went down there and measured the footprints and everything, and we stayed out here until about seven or eight o'clock at night, still wondering what it was. But they didn't say what it was or not. But nine o'clock, they said — we went down to a courthouse and we talked about it until about midnight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instantly Socorro was the center of an unprecedented media frenzy.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: This is one of the few sightings that got national attention immediately. Lonnie Zamora's story is on the national news, it's in all the newspapers, everybody's talking about it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Kevin D. Randle is an internationally renowned UFO investigator. He feels the Socorro events stand alone because of the amount of physical evidence collected at the scene.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Landing gear marks were found, the bush was burned by the UFO engine, there were occupants, creatures from the craft sighted by Lonnie Zamora, and the event brought the greatest UFO researcher of the day to Socorro. J. Allen Hynek, the Air Force consultant, came to Socorro. He looked at it, talked to Zamora, talked to Zamora's superiors, talked to people who saw the landing traces, took photographs. So there's physical evidence remaining behind — it's one of the few times they said there could be a flying saucer.

segments.speaker: Timmerman
segments.text: I had conversations with Dr. Hynek about the Socorro case, and his comments to me led me to believe that he felt that this was one of those cases where the government was unwilling to permit him to say what he would like to say about it. And that [inaudible] a great deal.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: According to John Timmerman, a longtime associate of J. Allen Hynek, the Socorro event was one of the defining moments in Hynek's career.

segments.speaker: Timmerman
segments.text: He felt that this was one of the most important cases he'd come across, and I think that maybe his attitude toward it was developed as a result of his feel about Lonnie Zamora, the primary witness.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: Lonnie Zamora is very credible. He's a police officer, he has nothing to gain by telling the story. He has stuck with this story from the very beginning: this is what he saw. There's no question that Lonnie Zamora saw something unusual on the ground.

segments.speaker: interviewee
segments.text: According to the Air Force and government, they say they don't know what it was, and they never told me not to say or [to] say about it, you know, talk about it. But they say that they don't know what it was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In fact, it took 21 years for the Air Force to finally offer an explanation for the Socorro UFO landing. They offered logs from the White Sands missile base charting government testing of the newly developed lunar landing module. But the logs indicate the tests ended more than five hours before Zamora's sighting.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The Air Force explanation simply doesn't work, because they have no documentation to place the lunar lander in that portion of New Mexico at that time. It does not match Zamora's description. I think if Dr. Hynek were here today and saw this new documentation available, the report that the Air Force says it was a lunar lander — if anything, that landed near Socorro — I think he'd say [bushwa]. He'd say that this is the government trying to do its fancy little dance and saying things that will satisfy the media, who will satisfy the country and the world, that there's no reality to the UFO phenomena. Whereas there is.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And according to the JPL in Pasadena, California, the lunar lander alluded to in the government data did not fly: it was dropped from a tower and had no system of independent propulsion, as reported by Zamora. Randle believes that this is proof the Socorro UFO was not a lunar lander.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: The Air Force completed their UFO investigation, said they had nothing more to say on it, and yet now they're coming out this year providing us with new explanations for old sightings. I have no idea why they're doing it, but I find it highly significant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Randle believes it is Socorro's proximity to several highly sensitive military bases that have prompted a continuing disinformation campaign.

segments.speaker: interviewer
segments.text: It is between the Los Alamos National Laboratory, the White Sands Missile Range; the Very Large Array radio telescope is 50 or 60 miles to the west. Socorro is right in the middle of this. If you've got a race of intelligent beings wanting to see what we're doing, this makes it a perfect place for them to come to observe our steps into space and what our science is doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: According to Timmerman, the Socorro event convinced Dr. Hynek that the truth about UFOs was being manipulated by the Air Force. After Socorro, Hynek left his post; the government lost one of its most prestigious spokespersons and gained its most ardent critic.

segments.speaker: Timmerman
segments.text: Dr. Hynek saw this, and it was very obvious to him that what Lonnie Zamora was saying, in the depths of his honesty, was not what the military was saying in their attempt to explain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Disproving the lunar lander theory does not mean that the Socorro craft came from another planet, but it does raise serious questions about the true nature of the event. What could have landed there more than 30 years ago that is still too sensitive to reveal?
